'Wall-to-Wall' Map of NYC Trees Could Help Cool Cities Worldwide

August 22, 2026 Caitlin Hayes, Cornell University urban forestry, tree mapping, lidar, satellite imagery, cooling, New York City, Cornell University, canopy, heat waves, Scientific Data
Read the source article

Quick summary

Researchers from Cornell University created the first "wall-to-wall" citywide map identifying 1.8 million individual trees in New York City — including 1.4 million never before surveyed — using satellite imagery, ground data, and lidar, with 82% accuracy, to optimize tree placement for urban cooling.

Key takeaways

  • First wall-to-wall citywide tree map identifying 1.8 million individual trees, 1.4 million of which had never been surveyed
  • Uses satellite imagery, on-the-ground datasets, and 3D lidar data with 82% overall accuracy
  • Covers private property, natural areas, and unsurveyed areas constituting an estimated 65% of the city's canopy
  • Part of the Cool Trees project optimizing tree placement for cooling as NYC heat waves become more frequent
  • NYC set a goal of expanding tree cover from 22% to 30% by 2040, which the map could directly inform
